references.text: The older son became angry and refused to go in. His anger reflects the attitude of the Pharisees and scribes who grumbled that Jesus welcomed sinners ([ref:Luk 15:2|Luke 15:2]). The parable is a direct response to their complaint.

The father's reaction—that he went out and pleaded with him—shows God's initiative toward the self-righteous, just as He seeks the lost ([ref:Luk 15:4|Luke 15:4]). The father actively approaches both sons.

Jonah's anger over God's mercy toward Nineveh mirrors the older son's anger at his father's grace toward the younger one ([ref:Jona 4:1-4|Jonah 4:1-4]). Both react negatively to God showing compassion to those they believe do not deserve it.

In the parable of the workers in the vineyard, those hired first grumble that the last arrivals receive equal pay ([ref:Matt 20:11-15|Matthew 20:11-15]). The same theme: dissatisfaction with God's generous grace toward others.

In the parable of the two sons, Jesus illustrates that tax collectors and sinners enter God's kingdom ahead of the self-righteous ([ref:Matt 21:28-31|Matthew 21:28-31]). Both parables contrast two types of sons and their responses to the father.

Paul describes Israel's jealousy that Gentiles share in God's grace ([ref:Rom 10:19-21|Romans 10:19-21]). This jealousy resembles the older son's anger at his father showing kindness to the younger son.

When the Jews in Antioch of Pisidia saw the crowds, they were filled with envy and contradicted Paul's preaching ([ref:Apg 13:45-46|Acts 13:45-46]). Their reaction illustrates the older son's attitude in practice.
The Pharisees' complaint that Jesus eats with tax collectors and sinners ([ref:Luk 5:30-32|Luke 5:30-32]) shows the same attitude as the older son—resistance to grace being extended to the unworthy.
God's thoughts and ways are higher than human ones ([ref:Jes 55:8-9|Isaiah 55:8-9]). The older son's anger reveals that he does not understand his father's heart or the greatness of grace.
